case_study_insert.main_stem: Voltwave Energy (VWE) is a public limited company in the renewable energy sector, installing rooftop solar systems, and employs a workforce of 80. Founded in 2013 by Priya Volt, the business serves commercial buildings and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VWE plans to invest $1,500,000 in a battery-storage assembly line, financed by an $800,000 bank loan and a $700,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $70, and produces 26,000 units a year. VWE faces two problems: a 4.5% defect rate in battery packs and a shortage of qualified electricians delaying new commercial installations.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report, Q4 2025: VWE assembled 6,500 battery units last quarter with a defect rate of 4.5%, down from 7.2% a year earlier. Installation rework jobs fell from 31 to 18 per month. Average install time is 5.6 days. A survey of 280 commercial property clients found 73% would pay a 6% premium for certified battery storage, and 61% value quick installation most. A skills audit shows 18 of 80 technicians lack electrical certification; accredited courses cost $1,400 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Voltwave Energy for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (March 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing interest on VWE's $800,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.50 an hour, lifting wage costs for VWE's 80 staff. (3) Lithium and solar-cell input prices rose 11.2% year-on-year, general inflation is 3.9%, and commercial electricity prices for customers fell 2.4%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for VWE of financing its $1,500,000 battery-storage line with a share issue rather than extra bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Money raised from the $700,000 share issue does not have to be repaid and carries no interest, so VWE can devote its cash to the $600,000 fixed costs and to reducing the 4.5% battery-pack defect rate without adding to the interest payable already on the $800,000 loan. For a public limited company, equity is a natural source of long-term capital for a $1,500,000 assembly line whose returns may take several years to arrive.

Point 2: Equity requires no collateral and cannot be repossessed if installation delays persist, so the new line and the commercial installations are not put at risk. It also spreads the financing risk between shareholders and lenders. Although existing shareholders are diluted, no cash leaves the business to service the capital, leaving more of the $30 contribution per unit to reinvest in training the 18 technicians who lack certification and in cutting the 5.6-day installation time that clients care about.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to VWE's financing choice and case data.

questions.question_text: VWE is launching its certified battery-storage systems. Consider trade exhibitions, social media campaigns, or partnerships with commercial property developers. Which should VWE choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade exhibitions: Industry exhibitions let VWE demonstrate the certified battery packs to technical buyers and network with installers, which suits a product with a 4.5% defect rate that buyers will want to inspect. However, stand costs and staff time are high, attendance is infrequent, and the audience is broad rather than the 280 commercial property clients already surveyed, so conversion may be slow for a business carrying $600,000 of fixed costs.

Social media campaigns: Social platforms can build awareness cheaply and target ads by job title or location, and short videos can show quick installation, which 61% of surveyed clients value most. The weakness is that complex technical claims about certification are hard to convey in a short post, and clicks do not necessarily become the large commercial orders needed to justify the $1,500,000 assembly line.

Partnerships with commercial property developers: Working directly with developers puts VWE in front of the exact buyers commissioning rooftop solar, and can be tied to the 73% of surveyed clients who would pay a 6% premium for certified storage. Joint bids make the 5.6-day installation promise credible and generate repeat projects. The drawback is dependence on a few partners and possible pressure on price, but the fit with the product and market is strong.

Recommendation: VWE should choose partnerships with commercial property developers. They reach the precise market in the survey, support a 6% premium and turn certification into a selling point, while exhibitions are rejected as costly and episodic and social media as too diffuse for large commercial contracts. VWE can use small social campaigns to support the partner-led sales effort.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to VWE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VWE with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context with a justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: VWE's battery-pack defect rate is 4.5% and a shortage of qualified electricians is delaying installations. Explain two benefits for VWE of using autocratic leadership to improve performance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership allows Priya Volt to impose one strict assembly checklist across the hierarchical structure, so all 80 staff follow the same testing routine. With the defect rate at 4.5% and rework jobs still at 18 a month, firm instructions and close inspection can cut faults fast, protecting the $70 selling price and the 73% of surveyed clients who will pay more for certified storage.

Point 2: Top-down decisions speed up the response to the electrician shortage. The audit shows 18 technicians without certification, and an autocratic leader can immediately allocate the $1,400 accredited courses and set deadlines without delay. Faster decisions also let VWE resequence the 5.6-day installations so skilled electricians work where they are most needed, reducing delays and defending the $30 contribution per unit. A consultative approach would take longer to agree testing routines, which suits neither the 4.5% defect target nor the 280 commercial clients demanding certified systems.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to VWE's defect, skills and installation data.

questions.question_text: VWE must train 18 technicians who lack electrical certification. Consider in-house on-the-job coaching or accredited external courses costing $1,400 per employee. Which should VWE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
In-house on-the-job coaching: Coaching on VWE's own assembly line teaches the exact battery-pack routines linked to the 4.5% defect rate, and the 18 technicians keep producing while they learn. It uses the knowledge of existing qualified electricians and costs no course fees, which helps with fixed costs of $600,000 a year. The weaknesses are that it depends on those electricians, who are already in short supply, it may repeat bad habits, and it gives no certificate, so the survey's demand for certified battery storage might not be met.

Accredited external courses: Sending all 18 technicians on the $1,400 course gives a recognised qualification and current electrical standards, directly closing the skills gap. The total of 18 × $1,400 = $25,200 is small against the $1,500,000 assembly line and can be funded from the $700,000 share issue. The cost is that 18 of 80 staff are away from the line, which could raise the 5.6-day installation time and affect the 26,000-unit target, and the generic course may need follow-up on VWE's own packs.

Decision: VWE should choose accredited external courses. The $25,200 cost is affordable and certification is what 73% of surveyed clients are paying a 6% premium for, so the qualification has direct commercial value. On-the-job coaching is rejected because it cannot confer certification and relies on the scarce electricians VWE is trying to replace with skilled staff. Lost production can be spread over several intakes. Running the $1,400 courses in two intakes would limit disruption to the 5.6-day installation schedule while still qualifying all 18 technicians.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training options with limited application to VWE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options using VWE's 18 staff, $1,400 and defect data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both options with shown cost arithmetic and a justified decision explaining why the alternative is rejected.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VWE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($70 − $40) = $600,000 ÷ $30 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $70 − $40 = $30. Answer: contribution per unit is $30.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VWE's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 20,000-unit break-even point with actual output of 26,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 6,000 units, so managers can judge how far sales could fall before the new line loses money.
2. Use the $30 contribution to test the 6% premium that 73% of surveyed clients would pay, estimating whether certification can lift effective price above $70 and lower break-even.
3. Check that the $800,000 bank loan and the $1,500,000 investment are serviceable: every unit above 20,000 adds $30 toward the $600,000 fixed costs and the $240,000 interest payable shown in the accounts.
4. Benchmark average total cost of about $63.08 a unit ($600,000 ÷ 26,000 + $40) each quarter to reveal the cost of the 4.5% defect rate and guide negotiations as lithium prices rise 11.2%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $30 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 6,000 units against 26,000 output; premium pricing from the 73% survey finding; loan-service feasibility on $800,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking near $63.08 to track defects and lithium prices.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VWE's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VWE's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 30.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $4,000,000 divided by revenue of $10,000,000 gives 40.0%; 2025 gross profit of $5,400,000 divided by $12,000,000 gives 45.0%. Operating profit of $1,500,000 divided by 2024 revenue gives 15.0%; 2025 operating profit of $2,400,000 divided by $12,000,000 gives 20.0%. Return on capital employed of $1,500,000 on $7,500,000 capital gives 20.0%; 2025 return of $2,400,000 on $8,000,000 gives 30.0%. Revenue grew 20.0% while cost of sales grew only 10.0%, and operating profit rose 60% against a 6.7% rise in capital employed.

Evaluation: All three measures improved strongly. The gross margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue outpaced cost of sales, suggesting VWE controlled lithium and battery costs despite a 4.5% defect rate. Operating return climbed from 15.0% to 20.0%, showing that fixed costs of $600,000 were absorbed more effectively as volumes grew. Returns on capital jumped from 20.0% to 30.0%, a valuable result because the $1,500,000 assembly line raises the capital base and shareholders will expect a return. Interest payable rose from $200,000 to $240,000, but operating profit grew far faster, so the $800,000 loan has not weakened performance. The limitation is that these figures predate the 11.2% rise in lithium and solar-cell prices.

Conclusion: VWE's profitability has clearly improved, and the improvement is robust because trading margins and the return on a slightly larger capital base both rose together. The main threat is that a 45.0% gross margin could be squeezed by input inflation, so management should defend the $30 contribution per unit and cut the 4.5% defect rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or trends with little or no accurate ratio calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with some relevant analysis of the trends.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest movements, and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VWE of promoting certified battery storage to commercial property clients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 280 commercial clients found that 73% would pay a 6% premium for certified battery storage and that 61% value quick installation most. Certification therefore lets VWE charge above the $70 selling price and increase the $30 contribution per unit, while the 5.6-day installation record supports the promise. This helps justify the $1,500,000 assembly line and gives developers a reason to choose VWE over competitors.

Disadvantage: Certification requires inspections and documented testing, which add to the $600,000 fixed costs and can slow the 5.6-day installation time. With the defect rate at 4.5%, any failed certification check could delay a commercial project and damage the 73% of clients willing to pay more. The $800,000 loan also needs servicing, so if the 6% premium is not accepted across all contracts, the extra compliance cost may not be recovered. If commercial developers insist on fixed prices, the 6% premium may not be realised on every contract, leaving VWE to absorb the inspection costs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed development using VWE's survey, cost and quality data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 4.5%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in lithium and solar-cell prices will affect VWE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If VWE's $800,000 loan is variable-rate, the increase is 0.75 percentage points, so 0.0075 × $800,000 = $6,000 a year. That is modest next to fixed costs of $600,000 and interest payable of $240,000, and it can be eliminated by fixing the rate. Higher rates could make future borrowing dearer, but the direct cash effect is small.

Minimum wage increase (7.1% to $13.50): VWE employs 80 staff and produces 26,000 units, so labour productivity is 26,000 ÷ 80 = 325 units per worker. Hours and individual pay are not given, so an annual wage-bill figure cannot be invented; the relevant test is whether productivity stays near 325 units or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $30 contribution narrows. The 18 technicians needing certification make training an additional cost pressure.

Lithium and solar-cell price rise (11.2%): The insert does not decompose the $40 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if all of it were affected, 11.2% × $40 = $4.48 per unit, and at 26,000 units that is 26,000 × $4.48 = $116,480 a year. Even a smaller share would reduce the $30 contribution, though the 2.4% fall in commercial electricity prices could support demand for solar systems.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in lithium and solar-cell prices will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 26,000 units, directly erodes the contribution that funds the $1,500,000 line, and cannot be hedged like the $6,000 interest change or offset as readily as a wage rise that productivity can absorb. The wage rise ranks second and the interest rise third.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to VWE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on VWE's costs or financing using case figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown arithmetic, a justified greatest-impact judgement on input prices, and reasons why the other two are smaller.
